candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — safe specimen transport
candidate.educational_objective: Before pneumatic-tube transport of an approved routine specimen, verify correct identification, secure closure, and facility-approved leak-resistant containment.

options.A: Confirm the specimen is correctly identified, securely closed, and placed in the facility-approved leak-resistant transport packaging for the pneumatic system.
options.B: Loosen the specimen cap so pressure changes during transport can escape through the container opening.
options.C: Remove patient identification because the pneumatic carrier itself provides sufficient specimen identity.
options.D: Place an unsealed specimen directly into the pneumatic carrier because the transport system prevents leakage by design.

candidate.rationale: CDC laboratory-safety guidance states that pneumatic-tube use should be governed by facility procedures and risk assessment because specimen breakage or leakage can contaminate the system. Specimens should be in intact, secure containers, and leakproof primary/secondary containment is a core transport principle. A is therefore appropriate for a routine specimen in a validated system. B and D deliberately increase leakage risk, and C creates an identification error.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Pneumatic-tube specimen transport requires SOP/risk assessment; unsealed containers can be inappropriate; leakage can contaminate the transport system; specimens should use leakproof containment.
candidate.source_document_title: Guidelines for Safe Work Practices in Human and Animal Medical Diagnostic Laboratories
